record_corrected: Relations were rewritten during wave-1 reconciliation after an automated evidence check found that 11 of this record's 13 original relations carried evidence strings that do not appear on the source page. Most were paraphrase; two were substantive errors. (a) The record asserted 'n1ql:automatic-reprepare-on-index-changes availableSince version:server-8-0' quoting 'In Couchbase Server 8.0 and later, the Query service automatically reprepares...'. No such sentence exists and the page states no version for this feature at all - the fabricated triple has been deleted, not re-evidenced. (b) The n1ql-feat-ctrl evidence read 'To disable this feature, set bit 23...' where the page reads 'To enable the feature, set bit 23...' - inverted polarity. (c) 'prepared statements are propagated to all query nodes in the cluster' was replaced by what the page actually says about cache priming. All evidence strings below are verified verbatim substrings of the source page.

notable_absence.finding: No edition gate on this page. Prepared statements, auto-prepare, auto_execute and both reprepare behaviours are all presented as edition-neutral, matching the function pages in this batch and contrasting with every index page (which all carry Enterprise gates for replica/storage features). Also absent, and more surprising: the page never states a privilege for PREPARE itself in its Prerequisites - the privilege facts are derived from the worked examples plus the general inheritance rule. Any extraction pipeline that scrapes only Prerequisites headings would record PREPARE as requiring no privileges at all, which is why inheritsPrivilegesFrom had to be minted. A third absence, established only by the post-hoc evidence check: the page states NO version for either reprepare behaviour, despite the opt-in extension reading like a recent addition. Its version status is unknown from this page alone.

cross_product_finding: OPEN ITEM 1, SETTLED - the Capella record's mapping is confirmed wrong, and in a way that is worth recording precisely because the error is not a naming quirk but a broken link. The Capella record cloud/n1ql/n1ql-language-reference/prepare.json carries a concept whose LABEL reads 'Query Update (privilege required under Advanced cluster access credentials, for a prepared UPDATE)' but whose candidate_id is privilege:capella-advanced-access-query-index. The correctly-named concept privilege:capella-advanced-access-query-update already exists as a promoted registry concept, so this is a mis-link to an existing sibling rather than a missing concept: the fix is a one-line id correction in the Capella record, and no new concept is needed. Per instructions that record has not been edited. Independently of the mis-link there is a real naming divergence on the read privilege: Server 8.0 says 'Query Select' where the Capella page says 'Query Read' for the same capability, which is exactly the phenomenon already filed as docs-issue cloud-n1ql-privilege-naming-inconsistency-select-vs-read - this page is a further instance of it and, usefully, an instance where the Server side can be quoted verbatim ('user must have the _Query Select_ privilege'). Reconciliation guidance: mint the Server privileges (privilege:query-select, privilege:query-update) in their own right and link them to their Capella twins with a mapping relation rather than merging them, because the underlying access models differ (Server RBAC roles/privileges vs Capella Basic/Advanced cluster access credentials) even where the English matches. Finally, the Capella page has no counterpart to the automatic-reprepare-on-index-changes section and no n1ql-feat-ctrl mention.
version_finding: REWRITTEN after the evidence check; the original version of this finding was built partly on a fabricated quote and reached a conclusion the page does not support. What the page actually contains: (1) TWO surviving 6.5 gates - the prepared statement cache ('In Couchbase Server 6.5 and later, the query engine uses the prepared statement cache to speed up the creation of prepared statements') and cache priming on node start/restart. These matter as control cases: the index pages in this batch lost five 7.2-era gates between 7.2 and 8.0, so gate attrition is not uniform, and reconciliation cannot assume a gate absent at 8.0 was never there. (2) A backward-compatibility retention: encoded_plan, 'included for backward compatibility', usable 'in versions of Couchbase Server prior to Couchbase Server 6.5'. This is the batch's clearest deprecation-shaped fact and yet the page never uses the word 'deprecated' - the whole batch has zero occurrences of deprecated/removed/superseded. So the wave's proposed deprecatedIn predicate has, on this evidence, no directly quotable instances anywhere in the batch, while retainedForLegacyCompatibility has two (here and alterindex.json). Recommendation unchanged: promote retainedForLegacyCompatibility as the extraction-time predicate, and treat deprecatedIn as a curated/inferred layer rather than an extracted one. (3) A version boundary used as the OBJECT of a non-availableSince predicate (encoded_plan retainedForLegacyCompatibility version:server-6-5) - so version: is not exclusively an availableSince range terminator. (4) NO 8.0 gate anywhere on the page, and no version at all attached to either reprepare behaviour. The original record asserted an 8.0 availableSince for automatic reprepare, and described it as 'a new 8.0 section' and 'the batch's clearest new-in-8.0 behavioural feature'; none of that is supported by the page text. This is the wave's most important methodological datum: a plausible, well-reasoned, confidently-annotated version gate was invented for exactly the kind of feature that looks new, on the page where the wave was most motivated to find one. Feature-flag gating and version gating are easy to conflate, because 'you must set a bit to enable it' reads like recency. The lesson for the remaining server waves is that availableSince assertions need mechanical evidence verification, not reviewer judgement.
